questions.q: If an attacker took one privileged account today, what could they reach?
questions.why: Puts a price on privilege before any tool is discussed.
questions.need: One stolen privileged account cannot reach everything
questions.how: Map what each privileged role can reach and cut what it does not need
questions.listen: "Everything" is honest and common; a clear limit means tiers and separate admin accounts already exist.
questions.probe: Which privileged account would hurt most, and who uses it every day?

questions.q: How long does it take to remove every access of someone who leaves?
questions.why: Offboarding time is the identity metric executives understand.
questions.need: Every access of a leaver is removed within a day
questions.how: Automate offboarding from the HR system
questions.listen: Same day across every system is the target; "the directory is quick, the apps are not" is the usual gap.
questions.probe: Which applications keep their own accounts outside the directory?

questions.q: How many directories and identity providers do you run, including the ones from acquisitions?
questions.why: Unconnected directories are where old accounts survive.
questions.need: Every directory and identity provider is known and connected
questions.how: List them, acquisitions included, and connect each one
questions.listen: Several directories are normal after acquisitions; what matters is that each is known and joined.
questions.probe: Which directory would an attacker use to reach the others?

questions.q: Do you know every account with administrative rights, human and machine?
questions.need: Every privileged account, human or machine, is known
questions.how: Build the privileged inventory and give each an owner
questions.listen: Machine accounts are usually the gap: count them as carefully as the people.
questions.probe: How many of those accounts have more rights than their task needs?

questions.q: Is strong multi-factor required for every privileged sign-in, with no exceptions list?
questions.need: Strong multi-factor protects every privileged sign-in, with no exceptions
questions.how: Close the exceptions list one account at a time
questions.listen: "Except" is the answer to listen for: the exceptions are where attacks get in.
questions.probe: Who is on the exceptions list, and since when?

questions.q: When were access rights last reviewed, and who signed the review?
questions.why: Unsigned reviews are paperwork, not control.
questions.need: Access is reviewed on a schedule, and someone signs
questions.how: Set a review cycle with named reviewers
questions.listen: Reviewed by the owner who knows the access, and something removed each time; otherwise it is a signature.
questions.probe: What did the last review remove?

questions.q: How many service accounts have passwords that never change?
questions.why: Static secrets are the quiet risk.
questions.how: Vault the secrets and set rotation
questions.listen: Secrets that never change are reused by attackers for years.
questions.probe: Which of those service accounts could reach production data?

questions.q: When a risky sign-in alert fires, who acts and how fast?
questions.why: Detection without an owner is noise.
questions.need: A risky sign-in alert is acted on quickly
questions.how: Agree who acts and how fast
questions.listen: Minutes, by a named team, with the power to block the session; otherwise the alert is a log line.
questions.probe: What did the last risky sign-in turn out to be, and how long did it take to know?
